title: Cost and Cost Effectiveness of ASSISTments Online Math Support: Analysis From a Randomized Controlled Study in Middle School
extended_summary:
This report examines the cost and cost-effectiveness of ASSISTments, an online math support platform, using data from a randomized controlled study in North Carolina middle schools. The central question is not only whether ASSISTments improves student math outcomes, but also what resources are required to implement it and whether those costs are reasonable relative to its educational impact.

The intervention was ASSISTments used primarily as an online homework tool for seventh-grade math, sometimes also for classwork. Students received immediate feedback on math problems, while teachers had access to real-time reports on student performance. Intervention teachers also received substantial implementation support, including 2-day in-person professional development before each school year and ongoing coaching during the year. Comparison schools continued business-as-usual math instruction and technology use without access to ASSISTments or related training.

The study took place in 63 schools across 41 districts in North Carolina, including many Title I schools and schools in rural, town, suburban, and urban settings. The broader trial enrolled 102 seventh-grade math teachers and more than 9,000 students. For the follow-up impact analysis, the analytic sample included 5,991 students whose eighth-grade state math test scores were available. The intervention was implemented across two school years (2018-19 and 2019-20), and outcomes were measured one year later using the 2021 North Carolina eighth-grade End-of-Grade math assessment.

The report concludes that ASSISTments produced a statistically significant positive long-term effect on math achievement, with an effect size of 0.10. The estimated incremental implementation cost was $46.23 per student for the full intervention sample, yielding a cost-effectiveness ratio of about $462.30 per student per standard deviation improvement. The authors argue that ASSISTments appears relatively low cost and cost-effective compared with other math interventions, especially intensive tutoring models, though results depend on implementation assumptions and some cost estimates relied on self-reported teacher data.

identified_tools.name: ASSISTments
identified_tools.description: Online mathematics practice and homework platform that delivers immediate feedback on student work, provides scaffolded support on problems, and gives teachers real-time reports on student progress and performance.
identified_tools.use_case: Deployed as an online homework support tool for 7th-grade mathematics in 63 North Carolina schools across 41 districts. Intervention teachers were expected to assign ASSISTments for 20–30 minutes at least twice weekly and review student data reports; many also used it for classwork. The randomized controlled trial enrolled 9,073 qualified students (4,495 intervention; 4,578 comparison), with the preregistered primary analytic sample consisting of 5,991 students who took the 8th-grade EOG math test (2,961 intervention; 3,030 comparison). Compared against business-as-usual math instruction, usual curriculum/homework practices, and existing technology tools other than ASSISTments.

findings.finding_summary: On the North Carolina 8th-grade End-of-Grade math test, intervention students scored 0.8 points higher than comparison students 1 year after implementation ended (estimated mean 535.13 vs. 534.33; p=0.011). The paper reports this as a statistically significant long-term positive impact corresponding to Hedges’s g=0.10 in the analytic sample of 5,991 students.
findings.measure: 8th-grade North Carolina End-of-Grade mathematics test (EOG-MA08) score

findings.finding_summary: The estimated incremental cost of implementing ASSISTments above business-as-usual was $207,794.34 across intervention schools, corresponding to $46.23 per student when spread across 4,495 students in intervention schools. Sensitivity analyses reported per-student costs of $70.18 for the analytic sample only, $17.85 for a 2-year model with no local coach, $25.86 for a no-warm-up model, and $8.85 for a no-warm-up/no-local-coach model.
findings.measure: Incremental implementation cost above business-as-usual; cost per participant

findings.finding_summary: Using the reported long-term achievement effect of 0.10 standard deviations and the primary cost estimate of $46.23 per participant, the paper calculates a cost-effectiveness ratio of $462.30 per student per standard deviation difference in long-term 8th-grade math performance. Sensitivity analyses yielded alternative CERs of 701.8, 178.5, 258.6, and 88.5 dollars per standard deviation under different cost assumptions.
findings.measure: Cost-effectiveness ratio (dollars per student per standard deviation difference on long-term EOG math performance)

quality_tier_rationale: This is a large randomized controlled trial with a policy-relevant delayed outcome measure, but there are some concerns for evidence quality because seventh-grade outcome data were unavailable, the main impact estimate came from a follow-up analytic sample smaller than the original randomized sample, and some implementation/cost inputs relied on self-reports.
impact_tier_rationale: The study found a statistically significant positive long-term effect on math achievement with Hedges's g = 0.10, which fits the 0.05-0.20 range for a green impact rating.
